subject: math

unit.title: Place value to 100
unit.essentialQuestion: How do the tens and the ones decide how big a number is?

title: Ordering numbers to 100
objectives: By the end, I can put a set of two-digit numbers in order, smallest first.

vocabulary.definition: arrange numbers from smallest to largest (or largest to smallest)
the least and the greatest in a set
a line of numbers in order that shows where each one lives
vocabulary.example: 25 sits far left of 52 on a 0–100 track

emphasize: Ordering is COMPARING, REPEATED: find the smallest (tens first), set it down, repeat.
A number track lets you SEE which comes first.
Watch equal-tens sets (50 vs 52 → compare ones).

misconceptions: stopping after one comparison instead of repeating
ordering by ones digits or by 'first digit' without justification
hooks: A dropped book with muddled page numbers — the story won't make sense until the pages go back in order.

video.title: Arrange the Numbers | Comparing And Ordering | Comparing and Ordering Digit Numbers for Kids | Math
video.watchTask: Before the video places each number, point to where YOU think it goes.

afterCheck.question: What did the video check first when arranging the numbers?

plan.goal: Book-fixer mission: muddled pages 52, 25, 50; retrieve the golden rule.
plan.note: The mission frame ('the story won't make sense') gives ordering a purpose.
plan.successCriteria: Child recalls 'look at the tens first'.

script.say: Oh no — someone dropped the book and the page numbers got muddled: 52, 25, 50! The pages must go smallest first or the story won't make sense. Can you be the book-fixer? … First, quick memory check: to compare two numbers, where do we look first?
script.adaptHints: Swap 'book' for comics/manga/a favourite story. Listen for 'the tens'.

stuckProtocol: If the rule is shaky: quick warm-up — 'which is bigger, 30 or 50?' with drawn rods.

plan.goal: Model 'find the smallest, set it down, repeat' on 52, 25, 50 — including the equal-tens moment.
plan.note: Narrate the repeated comparison explicitly; place each number on a number line as it's chosen.
plan.successCriteria: Child sees the two-step routine and the equal-tens tiebreak (50 before 52).

script.say: Watch my book-fixer routine. Step one: find the SMALLEST. Compare the tens: 52 has 5 tens, 25 has 2 tens, 50 has 5 tens. The smallest tens is 2 — so 25 goes first! Step two: repeat with what's left. 52 and 50… same tens! So the ones break the tie: 0 beats 2, so 50 comes next, then 52. Look at the track: 25… 50… 52. The story makes sense again!
script.adaptHints: Say 'find it, place it, repeat' rhythmically — it's the memorable routine.

blocks.title: Find the smallest, place it, repeat

plan.goal: Shared ordering of 41, 14, 40 — the child runs the routine with prompts.
plan.note: Child picks the smallest first (14), then handles the equal-tens pair 40/41.
plan.successCriteria: Child produces 14, 40, 41 and explains both steps.

script.say: Together now: 41, 14, 40. You're the fixer — which has the fewest tens? … Yes, 14! Placed. Now 41 and 40 are left — what do you notice about their tens? … A tie! So who breaks it? … The ones: 0 beats 1. Give me the full order, smallest first!
script.adaptHints: Wait for the child at each '…'. If they rush, ask them to justify each pick.

wrongAnswers.remedy: 40 and 41 have the same tens — which has fewer ones?

wrongAnswers.why: ordered largest-ish first or by ones
wrongAnswers.remedy: Smallest FIRST — which of the three has the fewest tens?

plan.note: The equal-tens pair 50/52 is the revealing part.
plan.successCriteria: Child orders 25, 50, 52 and justifies why 50 comes before 52.

script.say: Now fix the book pages all by yourself: 52, 25, 50 — smallest first. And be ready to tell me how you decided between 50 and 52!
script.adaptHints: After success, probe: 'How did you decide 50 comes before 52?'

wrongAnswers.remedy: 50 and 52 have the same tens — compare the ones. Which is smaller, 0 or 2?

wrongAnswers.why: pattern-matched the first digits without understanding
wrongAnswers.remedy: Put them on the track — which sits furthest left? Why?

plan.goal: Independent ordering: 3-number sets, then a 4-number set with equal tens; once secure, largest-first.
plan.note: Director draws from practiceBank, start level 2. Core mirrors the script: 33/13/31 then 62/26/60/66.
plan.successCriteria: Child orders a 4-number set with an equal-tens pair correctly and flips one set largest-first.

script.say: Book-fixer, you're hired! More muddled pages coming — some sets have FOUR pages, and one set wants biggest first. Find it, place it, repeat!
script.adaptHints: Frame sets as the child's interests (race positions, card collections). Never change the numbers.

stuckProtocol: Name why: 'we forgot to compare AGAIN after placing one.'
Drop to the track: place each number where it belongs on a 0–100 line.
One hint: 'Find just the smallest first.'
Re-ask with only two numbers, then add the third back.
Keep it safe: 'Mistakes show us what to practise — smaller step.'

plan.goal: Child teaches the ordering routine back; end on a win.
plan.note: Child-led recall; also close the unit — all four lessons connect.
plan.successCriteria: Child states: compare tens, pick smallest, repeat; ones if tens are equal.

script.say: Teach me how to order numbers smallest first — you're the teacher now! … That's it: compare the tens, pick the smallest, place it, repeat — and let the ones break ties. You used the number track to CHECK yourself instead of guessing — that's careful maths. And guess what: tens and ones, smashing, comparing, ordering — you've mastered the whole place-value toolbox!
script.adaptHints: Name the specific self-check you observed. This closes Unit 1 — celebrate the arc.

wrongAnswers.remedy: Smallest FIRST — which has the fewest tens?

hints: All tens, no ones — just count the rods.

reteach.say: Round numbers are the friendliest: 20, 50, 80 — two rods, five rods, eight rods. Small tower to tall tower.

block.explain: Tens first: 1 ten is the fewest — 19 is smallest even with its big 9.

wrongAnswers.remedy: Compare tens only: 4, 1, 3. Which is the fewest?
We want the SMALLEST — the fewest tens.

hints: Ignore the ones for now — just read the tens: 4, 1, 3.
The big 9 in 19 can't outvote its single ten.

reteach.say: The Lesson 3 trap is back! 19 looks big because of the 9, but it has just ONE ten. 1 ten < 3 tens < 4 tens, so 19 is the smallest.

wrongAnswers.remedy: 31 and 33 tie on tens — which has fewer ones, 1 or 3?
Tens first: 1, 3, 3 — who has the fewest?

hints: Then break the 31/33 tie with the ones.

reteach.say: Same digits everywhere — the routine saves us. Fewest tens: 13 goes first. Then 31 and 33 tie on tens; ones break it: 1 before 3. So 13, 31, 33.

practiceBank.skill: order four numbers with equal tens

block.prompt: Four pages this time — smallest first!

wrongAnswers.remedy: 60, 62, 66 all have 6 tens — order just their ones: 0, 2, 6.

wrongAnswers.why: left the small odd-one-out for last
wrongAnswers.remedy: Start over with step one: which of ALL FOUR has the fewest tens?

hints: One number has only 2 tens — it leads.
The three 6-tens numbers: order by ones (0, 2, 6).

reteach.say: 26 wins the first round easily — 2 tens. Then a triple tie: 60, 62, 66. Ones decide: 0, 2, 6. Order: 26, 60, 62, 66. Repeat the routine until every page is placed!

block.prompt: Flip it! LARGEST first this time.

wrongAnswers.remedy: Read the mission again — biggest leads this time. Which has the MOST tens?
Tens first even going down: 7 tens beats 6 tens.

hints: Same routine, opposite direction: find the LARGEST first.

reteach.say: Largest first is the same game backwards: most tens leads. 71 (7 tens), then 68 (6 tens — its big 8 can't help), then 17. The routine works both ways!

block.prompt: On a 0–100 number track, which number sits FURTHEST LEFT: 45, 54, 40?
block.explain: Furthest left = smallest. 40 and 45 share 4 tens; 0 ones beats 5, so 40 is leftmost.

wrongAnswers.remedy: 40 and 45 tie on tens — which has fewer ones, 0 or 5?
Left means SMALL on the track. Which is smallest?

hints: 40 vs 45: same tens — check the ones.

reteach.say: The track is a picture of order: small numbers live left, big numbers live right. 40, 45, 54 — so 40 sits furthest left.

practiceBank.skill: order four numbers with equal tens

block.prompt: The hardest muddle yet — smallest first!

wrongAnswers.remedy: 78 has 7 tens, 80 has 8 tens — tens first, always.
80, 87, 88 share 8 tens — order their ones: 0, 7, 8.

hints: Then three numbers tie on 8 tens — let the ones queue up: 0, 7, 8.

reteach.say: Two traps in one set! First: 78 vs 80 — seven tens loses to eight tens, whatever the ones say. Then the triple tie: 80, 87, 88 by ones. Full order: 78, 80, 87, 88.

block.prompt: I'm thinking of a number that fits BETWEEN 47 and 52 on the track — and it has 5 tens. Type one!

wrongAnswers.why: in range but ignored the 5-tens clue
wrongAnswers.remedy: Good spot on the track — but check the second clue: how many tens must it have?

wrongAnswers.why: has 5 tens but outside the range
wrongAnswers.remedy: Is 55 between 47 and 52 on the track? Walk it: 47… 52. Where's 55?

reteach.say: Two clues, one detective: between 47 and 52 live 48, 49, 50, 51. With 5 tens? Only 50 and 51. Either cracks the case!

practiceBank.skill: spot and fix a wrong order

block.prompt: A friend ordered these smallest first: 25, 52, 50. What went wrong?
options: 50 and 52 are swapped — same tens, so ones decide
block.explain: 50 and 52 share 5 tens; ones break the tie (0 < 2), so 50 must come before 52.

wrongAnswers.remedy: Zoom in on 52 and 50 — same tens. Which has fewer ones?

reteach.say: Checking someone else's order makes you the referee: walk pair by pair. 25 before 52 ✓. But 52 before 50? Same tens, and 2 ones is MORE than 0 — swap them! Correct order: 25, 50, 52.

adaptivity.levelUp: 2 consecutive correct → next level; at level 3, interleave (largest-first, between-clues, referee items).
adaptivity.levelDown: 2 misses on the same skill → reteach on the number track, then a level-1 round-numbers set.
adaptivity.masterySignal: 3+ correct across levels 2–3 including a 4-number set with an equal-tens pair, plus one largest-first flip → mastery ≥ 0.8 for 'ordering to 100'. This completes Unit 1 — trigger the end-of-unit check.
struggleProtocol: Name why ('we forgot to compare again' / 'the tie slipped').
Drop to the track: place each number on a 0–100 line one at a time.
One hint: 'Find just the smallest first.'
Re-ask with only two numbers, then add back.
Keep it safe: 'Mistakes show us what to practise — smaller step.'
adaptivity.personalization: Frame sets as race finishes, collection counts, or page numbers of a favourite book (LearnerModel.interests). Keep 'find it, place it, repeat' identical.
adaptivity.endOnSuccess: Finish on a winnable set; process praise for checking with the track; celebrate completing the whole place-value unit.

differentiation.support: Place every number on a 0–100 track to SEE the order; drop to two numbers when stuck; keep sets to round tens.
differentiation.stretch: Four+ numbers with several equal-tens; order the same set both directions; between-two-numbers riddles; referee someone else's wrong order.

extension: Number line on the floor — the character deals imaginary cards one at a time; the child says exactly where each slots among the ones already placed.
assessmentEvidence: Child orders a set of 3–4 two-digit numbers correctly, justifying with tens-first reasoning and handling at least one equal-tens pair.
revisitLater: Mixed ordering starter in the end-of-unit check and before Unit 2. End-of-Unit 1 check: (1) 38 = __ tens __ ones → 3, 8. (2) Partition 76 → 70 + 6. (3) Bigger: 27 or 72? → 72. (4) Order 52, 25, 50 → 25, 50, 52.
